subject: chemistry
title: Group 0: the noble gases
key_idea: The **noble gases** are unreactive because their atoms have a full outer shell, which is a stable arrangement of electrons. Their boiling points and densities increase going down the group. Their uses follow from being unreactive and, for helium, from having a low density.

sections.heading: Why the noble gases are unreactive

blocks.text: The elements in Group 0 are helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon. This section covers their electrons and their reactivity.

items.meaning: The elements in Group 0 of the periodic table.
Does not react. The noble gases are unreactive.
An outer shell holding as many electrons as it can. This is a stable arrangement of electrons.

items: The noble gases have eight electrons in their outer shell, except helium, which has two.
A full outer shell is a stable arrangement of electrons.
The atoms do not gain, lose or share electrons, so they do not easily form molecules or compounds.
A sample of a noble gas is made of single atoms.
Noble gases have a full outer shell: 8 electrons, or 2 for helium.
This is a stable arrangement, so they do not gain, lose or share electrons.
They are unreactive and do not easily form compounds.

blocks.text: The boiling points of the noble gases increase going down the group, with increasing relative atomic mass.

items.text: The boiling points rise as you go down the group.
Xenon is below krypton in the group.
The boiling point of xenon is higher than that of krypton (−153 °C).

items: The density of the noble gases also increases going down the group. In order of increasing density: helium, neon, argon, krypton.
To predict a missing value, it lies between the values of the elements above and below it.
Boiling points and densities increase going down Group 0.
Use the pattern to predict values for other noble gases.

blocks.text: Each use of a noble gas depends on a property: being unreactive, having a low density or not being flammable.

diagram.alt: Tap a noble gas to learn its properties and uses, then test yourself.

parts.name: Helium
parts.detail: Unreactive, with the lowest density and boiling point (−269 °C). It is used in balloons and airships because it is less dense than air and will not ignite.

parts.name: Neon
parts.detail: Electronic structure 2,8, so a full outer shell. It is unreactive and does not form compounds. Its boiling point is −246 °C.

parts.name: Argon
parts.detail: Electronic structure 2,8,8. It is used to fill filament light bulbs and as an inert atmosphere for welding steel, because it does not react with the hot metal.

parts.name: Krypton
parts.detail: Unreactive but much denser than air, so it would not float in an airship. Its boiling point is −153 °C.

parts.name: Xenon
parts.detail: Below krypton in the group, so its boiling point and density are higher than krypton's.

items: Helium fills balloons and airships because it is less dense than air. It is also non-flammable.
Hydrogen is not used in airships because it is flammable and could ignite.
Krypton is not used in airships because it is more dense than air, so the airship would not float.
Argon fills filament light bulbs because it does not react with the hot metal filament. Oxygen in air would react with the filament to form a metal oxide.
Argon is used as an inert atmosphere for joining steel by heating, because it is unreactive.
Helium is used in balloons because it is less dense than air and non-flammable.
Argon is used when a reactive gas such as oxygen must be kept away, because it is inert.
For each use, name the property that makes the gas suitable.

checks.q: Explain, in terms of electrons, why argon is unreactive.
checks.a: Argon has a full outer shell of eight electrons, which is a stable arrangement. It does not gain, lose or share electrons.

checks.q: State the trend in the boiling points of the noble gases going down Group 0.
checks.a: The boiling points increase going down the group.

checks.q: State one property of helium, apart from being inert, that makes it suitable for filling balloons.
checks.a: It is less dense than air.

exam_phrases: argon has a full outer shell (of electrons)
argon has eight outer shell electrons
does not gain / lose / share electrons
the boiling points increase down the group

mistakes.wrong: Argon is unreactive because it has no outer shell electrons.
mistakes.right: This is ignored, and it is wrong. Argon has a full outer shell of eight electrons.

mistakes.wrong: No product forms because argon is a noble gas.
mistakes.right: 'Argon is a noble gas' is ignored. Explain with electrons: a full outer shell or a stable arrangement of electrons, so argon is unreactive.

mistakes.wrong: Argon is unreactive because it has a full outer shell, and that is all.
mistakes.right: Two marks need two ideas: a full outer shell (or eight electrons), and so a stable arrangement, or it does not gain, lose or share electrons.

worked_example.question:
Argon is an element in Group 0 of the periodic table.

Explain why argon is unreactive.
answer_points: Argon has a full outer shell of electrons (eight outer shell electrons is also accepted).
So argon has a stable arrangement of electrons, or it does not gain, lose or share electrons.
worked_example.tip: One mark for the full outer shell and one for the stable arrangement.

exam_phrases: (the gas atoms) have full outer shell(s)
so they do not gain / lose / transfer / share electrons
krypton is more dense than air, so the airship would not float
argon is unreactive, so it does not react with the metal filament

mistakes.wrong: Helium is suitable for balloons because it is light and not poisonous.
mistakes.right: Light and non-toxic are ignored. Say helium is less dense than air.

mistakes.wrong: The gases are inert because they do not react or gain a charge.
mistakes.right: 'Does not react' and 'does not gain a charge' are ignored. Say the atoms do not gain, lose, transfer or share electrons.

mistakes.wrong: The noble gases are inert because they have eight electrons.
mistakes.right: Mentions of numbers of electrons are ignored. Say the atoms have a full outer shell.

worked_example.question:
Helium, hydrogen and krypton are gases.

The table shows the reactivity and density, at room temperature and pressure, of helium, hydrogen and krypton.

Helium: unreactive, density 0.00018 g/cm³
Hydrogen: very reactive, density 0.00009 g/cm³
Krypton: unreactive, density 0.00380 g/cm³

The density of air is 0.001225 g/cm³.

Helium is used in airships.

Explain why hydrogen and why krypton are not used in airships.
answer_points: Hydrogen is flammable and could ignite.
Krypton is more dense than air (it has a high density).
So a krypton airship would not float.
worked_example.tip: Compare each density with the density of air, which is 0.001225.

exam_phrases: no tendency to lose or gain electrons
Group 1 elements do not have a full outer shell / have 1 electron in the outer shell

mistakes.wrong: The noble gases have no tendency to react.
mistakes.right: This is ignored unless it is linked to a full outer shell. Say they have a full outer shell, so no tendency to lose or gain electrons.

mistakes.wrong: Argon is 2,8,8 so it is unreactive.
mistakes.right: State the reason as well as the answer: it is unreactive because it has a full outer shell of electrons.

worked_example.question:
The elements in Group 0 (the noble gases) are unreactive.

Explain why, in terms of their electronic configurations.
answer_points: Group 0 elements have a full (complete) outer shell. Eight electrons in the outer shell is also accepted.
So they have no tendency to lose or gain electrons.
worked_example.tip: One mark for the full outer shell and one for the idea that they do not lose or gain electrons.
